newsitem.title: CANADA: Bank of Canada sees stronger growth in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Canada sees stronger growth in 1997.

text.p: Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen said Canada's economic growth will accelerate in 1997 while inflation remains low, according to minutes of the central bank's Board of Directors meeting held December 5.
In the minutes, released on Wednesday, Thiessen said the external environment was expected to support the expansion of the Canadian economy in the period ahead.

"The Governor said that, although the strike at General Motors was expected to have a noticeable impact on the level of output in the fourth quarter, external and domestic factors suggested that the economy had probably expanded appreciably during the quarter and would gather further momentum in 1997," the minutes said.

Thiessen also noted that with slackness in product and labor markets likely to remain an important factor in coming quarters, trend inflation was expected to stay in the lower part of the central bank's 1.0-3.0 percent target range.

Financial markets had increased their focus on Canada's positive fundamentals, Thiessen noted. He said growing awareness of Canada's improved fundamentals had helped to underpin the value of the Canadian dollar and facilitate a further significant decline in interest rates across the maturity curve since mid-October.
In a portion of the minutes devoted to domestic economic developments, the central bank noted both the consumer price index and so-called core CPI remain below 2.0 percent.

"Core inflation (measured by the year-over-year increase in the CPI excluding food, energy and the effect of indirect taxes) was only 1.3 percent and is expected to remain low, consistent with the sizable economic slack and the absence of cost pressures. Measured inflation may also be lower in the coming year as a result of the price-level effects of the recent appreciation of the Canadian dollar."
